queries.text: How did American cities change across four decades (1980-2024): gentrification, inequality, affordability, and displacement — every claim cited?
Median home price in major US metro areas 1980 vs 2024
Percentage change in median household income by decile in top 50 US cities 1980 to 2023
Gini coefficient for urban households in the United States annually from 1979 to 2022
Share of housing costs as a percentage of gross income (cost burden) for renters and owners in US metros 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020
Number of displaced households due to rising rents or property taxes in major gentrifying neighborhoods per year 1990-2023
Percentage change in median rent in high-gentrification census tracts vs low-gentrification tracts 1985-2024
Count of new luxury condominium units built versus affordable housing units subsidized by government in top 20 US cities annually from 1980 to present
Ratio of white residents to Black and Hispanic residents in specific gentrified neighborhoods (e.g., Brooklyn Heights, Pilsen) 1980 Census data compared to 2020 Census data
Median income growth rate for bottom quintile vs top quintile households in New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago 1983-2023
Percentage share of urban population living below the poverty line in designated opportunity zones or revitalization areas before and after major development projects

search_hits.title: Urban Gentrification Metrics: Four Decades of American City Transformation (the exemplar report)
search_hits.snippet: The operator's exemplar report (vendored as source-report.pdf): New York City leads with a Gini coefficient of 0.5469 versus the national average of 0.40 in 2013, while Atlanta and Miami follow at 0.57 and New Orleans at 0.56; the Case-Shiller Index reached 325.78 in July 2024 (+225% since January 2000); 48 of the 50 largest metros saw worsening mobility with Houston the sole improvement (+1.1%).

search_hits.title: Gentrification in America
search_hits.snippet: Governing analyzed Census tract data for the nation's 50 largest cities. Portland (58.1% of eligible tracts), Washington D.C. (51.9%), Minneapolis (50.6%), and Seattle (50%) led; nearly 20 percent of lower-income neighborhoods gentrified since 2000, compared to 9 percent in the 1990s; poverty rate percentage-point change -0.7 gentrifying vs +6.7 not gentrifying.
